Vietnam. A Southeast Asian nation stretching along the eastern coast of Indochina, bordered by China to the north and Cambodia and Laos to the west. Shaped by centuries of Chinese influence, French colonialism, and Cold War conflict—most devastatingly the Vietnam War from nineteen fifty-five to nineteen seventy-five—Vietnam embodies the geopolitics of twentieth-century Asia. The Mekong River Delta in the south makes it one of the world's leading rice producers and a vital player in regional water diplomacy.

The Mekong Delta in southern Vietnam is one of the world's richest agricultural regions, producing rice for both domestic consumption and export. It is Asia's rice bowl. Vietnam was historically dominated by China, resisting Chinese rule for nearly a millennium before establishing independence in nine hundred thirty-eight and maintaining it through a series of dynastic kingdoms. France colonized Vietnam from eighteen eighty-seven to nineteen fifty-four, making it part of French Indochina. French rule extracted resources and instilled colonial rivalries that persisted after independence.

The Vietnam War from nineteen fifty-five to nineteen seventy-five was fought between the communist North, supported by the Soviet Union and China, and the non-communist South, supported by the United States. The war killed an estimated two to three million people. The Tet Offensive in nineteen sixty-eight was a major turning point, demonstrating North Vietnamese military strength and shifting American and global public opinion decisively against the conflict. Vietnam unified under communist rule in nineteen seventy-five. Since nineteen eighty-six, economic reforms known as Doi Moi have transformed Vietnam into a market-oriented economy while maintaining one-party political control. Today Vietnam is a key player in Southeast Asian geopolitics and economics, with significant agricultural output, manufacturing capacity, and influence on regional trade and security.
